claim: The developed feedback-based tracking microscope can follow individual mitochondria in sensory neurons of zebrafish larvae with nanometer precision and millisecond temporal resolution.
source: We present the development and in vivo application of a feedback-based tracking microscope to follow individual mitochondria in sensory neurons of zebrafish larvae with nanometer precision and millisecond temporal resolution.
evidence: The abstract directly states the capabilities of the developed microscope system, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Individual mitochondria were tracked with unprecedented spatiotemporal resolution over distances of >100 µm.
source: By combining various technical improvements, we tracked individual mitochondria with unprecedented spatiotemporal resolution over distances of >100 µm.
evidence: The abstract states this achievement, which is demonstrated in the results section with trajectory data.

claim: Five distinct motional states were discriminated: a fast and a slow directional motion state in both the anterograde and retrograde directions and a stationary state.
source: Using these nanoscopic trajectory data, we discriminated five motional states: a fast and a slow directional motion state in both the anterograde and retrograde directions and a stationary state.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by detailed analysis in Figure 2 and associated data.

claim: After a pause, mitochondria predominantly persist in the original direction of travel.
source: The transition pattern revealed that, after a pause, mitochondria predominantly persist in the original direction of travel, while transient changes of direction often exhibited longer pauses.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by transition probability analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Transient changes of direction often exhibited longer pauses.
source: The transition pattern revealed that, after a pause, mitochondria predominantly persist in the original direction of travel, while transient changes of direction often exhibited longer pauses.
evidence: The abstract states this observation, which is quantified in the transition analysis showing decay constants of 3.2 s for slow-slow transitions versus 1.94-1.97 s for fast-fast or fast-slow transitions.

claim: Mitochondria in the vicinity of a second, stationary mitochondria displayed an increased probability to pause.
source: Moreover, mitochondria in the vicinity of a second, stationary mitochondria displayed an increased probability to pause.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by the analysis in Figure 3 showing increased stationary time when stationary mitochondria are present on the track.

claim: The basic molecular players of the axonal transport machinery are well established.
source: While the basic molecular players of the axonal transport machinery are well established (Hirokawa et al., 2010), the higher order levels of regulation that govern the overall 'life cycle' of axonal organelles are poorly understood (Misgeld and Schwarz, 2017; Plucińska and Misgeld, 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Hirokawa et al., 2010.

claim: The higher order levels of regulation that govern the overall 'life cycle' of axonal organelles are poorly understood.
source: While the basic molecular players of the axonal transport machinery are well established (Hirokawa et al., 2010), the higher order levels of regulation that govern the overall 'life cycle' of axonal organelles are poorly understood (Misgeld and Schwarz, 2017; Plucińska and Misgeld, 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Misgeld and Schwarz, 2017 and Plucińska and Misgeld, 2016.

claim: Proper distribution and turn-over of mitochondria are of seminal importance for neuronal homeostasis.
source: One example of this dearth of understanding is provided by mitochondria where their proper distribution and turn-over are of seminal importance for neuronal homeostasis (Chang and Reynolds, 2006; Sheng and Cai, 2012; MacAskill and Kittler, 2010; Saxton and Hollenbeck, 2012).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations: Chang and Reynolds, 2006; Sheng and Cai, 2012; MacAskill and Kittler, 2010; Saxton and Hollenbeck, 2012.

claim: Specific kinesin and dynein motors play well-established roles in the long-distance transport of axonal mitochondria.
source: Despite the well-established roles of specific kinesin and dynein motors in the long-distance transport of axonal mitochondria and some recent progress on the mechanisms of their local anchorage and degradation (MacAskill and Kittler, 2010; Saxton and Hollenbeck, 2012; Sheng, 2014; Ashrafi and Schwarz, 2013), many details regarding how the distribution of how mitochondria are established, maintained and regulated – especially in vivo – remain elusive.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to MacAskill and Kittler, 2010; Saxton and Hollenbeck, 2012; Sheng, 2014; Ashrafi and Schwarz, 2013.

claim: Many details regarding how the distribution of mitochondria are established, maintained and regulated in vivo remain elusive.
source: Despite the well-established roles of specific kinesin and dynein motors in the long-distance transport of axonal mitochondria and some recent progress on the mechanisms of their local anchorage and degradation (MacAskill and Kittler, 2010; Saxton and Hollenbeck, 2012; Sheng, 2014; Ashrafi and Schwarz, 2013), many details regarding how the distribution of how mitochondria are established, maintained and regulated – especially in vivo – remain elusive.
evidence: The statement is made in the context of discussing current knowledge gaps, supported by the citations provided.

claim: The regulatory interplay of molecular motors that propel and brake mitochondria and give rise to their characteristic 'saltatory' movement is not well understood.
source: For example, the regulatory interplay of molecular motors that propel and brake mitochondria and give rise to their characteristic 'saltatory' movement (Morris and Hollenbeck, 1993) and additional 'non-canonical' movement behaviors (Chang and Reynolds, 2006; Morris and Hollenbeck, 1993; Ligon and Steward, 2000) is not well understood.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Morris and Hollenbeck, 1993; Chang and Reynolds, 2006; Ligon and Steward, 2000.

claim: Mitochondria exhibit characteristic 'saltatory' movement.
source: For example, the regulatory interplay of molecular motors that propel and brake mitochondria and give rise to their characteristic 'saltatory' movement (Morris and Hollenbeck, 1993) and additional 'non-canonical' movement behaviors (Chang and Reynolds, 2006; Morris and Hollenbeck, 1993; Ligon and Steward, 2000) is not well understood.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Morris and Hollenbeck, 1993.

claim: Understanding of the origin, travel range and final destination of transported mitochondria is only emerging.
source: Our understanding of the origin, travel range and final destination of transported mitochondria is only emerging (Misgeld et al., 2007; O'Toole et al., 2008), and how the local cellular microenvironment, such as activity or calcium levels, influences mitochondrial motility in axons with a realistic in vivo geometry and surrounding is only now starting to be explored (Faits et al., 2016; Sajic et al., 2013; Ohno et al., 2011; Smit-Rigter et al., 2016; Lewis et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Misgeld et al., 2007 and O'Toole et al., 2008.

claim: How the local cellular microenvironment influences mitochondrial motility in axons with realistic in vivo geometry is only now starting to be explored.
source: Our understanding of the origin, travel range and final destination of transported mitochondria is only emerging (Misgeld et al., 2007; O'Toole et al., 2008), and how the local cellular microenvironment, such as activity or calcium levels, influences mitochondrial motility in axons with a realistic in vivo geometry and surrounding is only now starting to be explored (Faits et al., 2016; Sajic et al., 2013; Ohno et al., 2011; Smit-Rigter et al., 2016; Lewis et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Faits et al., 2016; Sajic et al., 2013; Ohno et al., 2011; Smit-Rigter et al., 2016; Lewis et al., 2016.

claim: There is a gap in understanding between the molecular underpinnings of mitochondrial transport from in vitro biophysical studies and the bigger picture of organelle homeostasis in neurons in vivo.
source: In many respects, the gap in understanding between the well-established molecular underpinnings of mitochondrial transport gleaned from biophysical studies in vitro and the bigger picture of this organelle's homeostasis in neurons in vivo can be attributed to a lack of techniques that can span the different spatial domains involved: Motors step on the scale of nanometers but propel organelles on the scale of many hundreds of micrometers.
evidence: The statement is made as an inference from the current state of the field and the technical limitations.

claim: Motors step on the scale of nanometers but propel organelles on the scale of many hundreds of micrometers.
source: In many respects, the gap in understanding between the well-established molecular underpinnings of mitochondrial transport gleaned from biophysical studies in vitro and the bigger picture of this organelle's homeostasis in neurons in vivo can be attributed to a lack of techniques that can span the different spatial domains involved: Motors step on the scale of nanometers but propel organelles on the scale of many hundreds of micrometers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about motor proteins and organelle transport distances.

claim: The approach based on 3D single particle tracking is suitable to bridge the spatial scale chasm between motor steps and organelle transport.
source: Here, we present an approach based on 3D single particle tracking (3D SPT) that is suitable to bridge this chasm and demonstrate the in vivo applicability of this tool to the zebrafish model of axonal transport (O'Donnell et al., 2013; Plucińska et al., 2012).
evidence: The statement is supported by the experimental demonstration in the manuscript and citations to O'Donnell et al., 2013 and Plucińska et al., 2012.

claim: A number of 3D SPT methods have been developed in the past few years.
source: In the past few years, a number of 3D SPT methods have been developed. They rely on different approaches like altering the shape of the point spread function (Spille et al., 2015; Kao and Verkman, 1994; Shechtman et al., 2015) or 'lock-in' feedback loops that re-center the laser focus onto the tracked particle (Welsher and Yang, 2014; Dupont et al., 2013; McHale et al., 2007; Perillo et al., 2015; Juette and Bewersdorf, 2010; Levi et al., 2005).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to different 3D SPT methods.

claim: 3D SPT techniques have largely remained restricted to cells in dissociated culture and other reductionist models due to technical limitations.
source: These approaches have established 3D SPT as a powerful tool to study the dynamics of subcellular structures. However, these techniques have largely remained restricted to cells in dissociated culture and other reductionist models due to technical limitations.
evidence: The statement is made as an assessment of the current state of the field based on the literature.

claim: The shape of each mitochondrion changes during transport along the neuron due to fusion and fission events.
source: First, due to fusion and fission events, the shape of each mitochondrion is changing during the transport along the neuron and thus the tracking technique must be resilient to such shape changes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: Transport in axons potentially extends over distances of hundreds of micrometers, even in a small organism like a fish larva.
source: Second, transport in axons, even in a small organism like a fish larva, potentially extends over distances of hundreds of micrometers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about axonal transport distances.

claim: The 3D SPT method combines high spatial (XY:<5 nm Z:<30 nm) and temporal resolution (100 Hz) with simultaneous wide-field imaging and local photo-activation.
source: Here, we present a 3D SPT method based on real-time 3D orbital tracking that is able to overcome these challenges: The method combines high spatial (XY:<5 nm Z:<30 nm) and temporal resolution (100 Hz) with simultaneous wide-field imaging and local photo-activation.
evidence: The statement describes the technical specifications of the developed method, which are demonstrated in the results.

claim: A feedback loop recurrently re-centers the specimen on top of the microscope once a tracked particle approaches the edge of the field of view.
source: A feedback loop recurrently re-centers the specimen on top of the microscope once a tracked particle approaches the edge of the field of view.
evidence: This describes a technical feature of the microscope system that is implemented and demonstrated.

claim: Single neuronal mitochondria can be tracked in vivo over distances of more than 100 µm using the combination of the tracking system and genetic tools.
source: In combination with previously developed genetic tools (Plucińska et al., 2012), we are capable of tracking single neuronal mitochondria in vivo over distances of more than 100 µm.
evidence: The statement is supported by the experimental data presented and citation to Plucińska et al., 2012.

claim: The microscope system revealed a previously undetected motional state in both the antero- and retrograde directions.
source: The exquisite spatiotemporal resolution of the microscope system allowed us to discriminate not only the canonical fast components during active motion, but also revealed a previously undetected motional state in both the antero- and retrograde directions.
evidence: The statement is supported by the analysis of trajectory data showing distinct slow movement states.

claim: The previously undetected motional state has a slower velocity and was engaged when mitochondria undergo temporary directional changes.
source: The exquisite spatiotemporal resolution of the microscope system allowed us to discriminate not only the canonical fast components during active motion, but also revealed a previously undetected motional state in both the antero- and retrograde directions. This state has a slower velocity and was engaged when mitochondria undergo temporary directional changes.
evidence: The statement is supported by the analysis of velocity distributions and transition patterns in Figure 2.

claim: A detailed examination of transitions between motion states and pause durations showed a complex pattern governing transient changes in mitochondrial motility.
source: A detailed examination of transitions between motion states and pause durations showed a complex pattern governing such transient changes in mitochondrial motility.
evidence: The statement is supported by the transition probability analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stationary mitochondria can act as roadblocks that initiate the slower motional state in passing organelles.
source: The combination of trajectory and 'environmental' data (i.e. wide-field images of the region surrounding the tracked particle) allowed us to analyze the influence of other mitochondria present in the axon and showed that stationary mitochondria can act as roadblocks that initiate the slower motional state in passing organelles, a potential mechanism for overcoming such physiological obstacles.
evidence: The statement is supported by the analysis in Figure 3 showing increased slow movement states when stationary mitochondria are present.

claim: The localization precision was <3 nm laterally and <21 nm axially for count rates above 200 photons per orbit (or 40 kHz) using stationary particles.
source: From the standard deviation of the particle position, we estimate the tracking accuracies to be <3 nm laterally and <21 nm axially for count rates above 200 photons per orbit (or 40 kHz).
evidence: The statement is supported by calibration measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For count rates of 1600 photons per orbit (or 320 kHz), no significant degradation of tracking was observed up to velocities of >25 µm/s laterally and 15 µm/s axially for moving particles.
source: For count rates of 1600 photons per orbit (or 320 kHz), no significant degradation of the tracking was observed up to velocities of >25 µm/s laterally and 15 µm/s axially.
evidence: The statement is supported by dynamic precision measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For a count rate of 500 photons per orbit (100 kHz), the in vivo localization precision along the minor axis of a stationary mitochondrion was 21 nm.
source: For a count rate of 500 photons per orbit (100 kHz), we measured a localization precision along the minor axis of the mitochondrion of 21 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The statement is supported by in vivo calibration measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The average localization precision for moving mitochondria after smoothing was 4.6 nm.
source: If we analyzed the standard deviation of the y orbit displacement (Figure 2c), we achieve an average localization precision of 4.6 nm after removing high-frequency noise by smoothing the trajectory data by five points.
evidence: The statement is supported by analysis of the orbit displacement data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Fast anterograde motion has an average velocity of 0.62 µm/s.
source: Fast states are responsible for long-distance trafficking of the mitochondria with average velocities of 0.62 µm/s for anterograde motion and 0.72 for retrograde motion.
evidence: The statement is supported by velocity analysis shown in Figure 2f and Table 1.

claim: Fast retrograde motion has an average velocity of 0.72 µm/s.
source: Fast states are responsible for long-distance trafficking of the mitochondria with average velocities of 0.62 µm/s for anterograde motion and 0.72 for retrograde motion.
evidence: The statement is supported by velocity analysis shown in Figure 2f and Table 1.

claim: The slow movement states carry out movements over shorter distances and shorter timescales than fast states.
source: The slow states carry out movements over shorter distances and shorter timescales (Figure 2c–f).
evidence: The statement is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2c-f comparing duration and displacement of fast and slow states.

claim: The characteristics of the slow movement states (duration, displacement and velocity) are similar in both directions.
source: The characteristics of the slow movement states (i.e. duration, displacement and velocity) are similar in both directions (Figure 2c).
evidence: The statement is supported by the comparison of slow anterograde and slow retrograde states in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Pauses involving fast motion states show mono-exponential distributions with decay constants of 1.94 s and 1.97 s.
source: Pauses involving fast motion states (fast-fast or fast-slow/slow-fast transitions) show mono-exponential distributions with decay constants of 1.94 s and 1.97 s, whereas pauses between two slow states show a longer duration with a decay constant of 3.2 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The statement is supported by the pause duration analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pauses between two slow states show a decay constant of 3.2 s.
source: Pauses involving fast motion states (fast-fast or fast-slow/slow-fast transitions) show mono-exponential distributions with decay constants of 1.94 s and 1.97 s, whereas pauses between two slow states show a longer duration with a decay constant of 3.2 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The statement is supported by the pause duration analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Very long pauses (>20 s) were always (98% of n = 97) associated with transitions involving the slow motion states.
source: Very long pauses (>20 s) were always (98% of n = 97) associated with transitions involving the slow motion states and had a high probability of involving a change in directionality (56% of n = 97).
evidence: The statement is supported by statistical analysis of pause durations and associated transitions.

claim: Very long pauses (>20 s) had a high probability of involving a change in directionality (56% of n = 97).
source: Very long pauses (>20 s) were always (98% of n = 97) associated with transitions involving the slow motion states and had a high probability of involving a change in directionality (56% of n = 97).
evidence: The statement is supported by statistical analysis of pause durations and directional changes.

claim: For pauses <20 s, a change in direction was only detected in 19% (of n = 1137) of the events.
source: For pauses <20 s, a change in direction was only detected in 19% (of n = 1137) of the events.
evidence: The statement is supported by statistical analysis of pause durations and directional changes.

claim: No transitions between fast anterograde and fast retrograde states were observed within one track.
source: We did not observe any transitions between fast anterograde and fast retrograde states within one track, not even multi-step transitions that would involve the slow state.
evidence: The statement is supported by analysis of all transitions in the trajectory data.

claim: Moving mitochondria have a high probability of continuing in the same direction after a pause (77% or higher depending on the mode of motion).
source: Moreover, moving mitochondria – irrespective of their speed – have a high probability of continuing in the same direction after a pause (77% or higher depending on the mode of motion, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The statement is supported by the transition probability analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Directional changes between fast and slow motion were unlikely (~6% of all pauses).
source: Approximately half of the time, the mitochondria remain in the same motional state (i.e. direction and velocity) and directional changes between fast and slow motion were unlikely (~6% of all pauses).
evidence: The statement is supported by the transition probability analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: When stationary mitochondria were present on the track, the time spent in the stationary state substantially increased in both directions (anterograde: 34% to 58%, retrograde: 40% to 58%).
source: However, when stationary mitochondria were present on the track, the time spent in the stationary state substantially increased in both directions (anterograde: 34% to 58%, retrograde: 40% to 58%).
evidence: The statement is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3b comparing free track versus occupied track conditions.

claim: For anterograde transport, the time spent in the fast movement state decreased substantially at sites occupied by resting mitochondria (ratio fast/slow movement states: free track - 56%/10% = 5.6 vs. occupied track - 27%/14% = 1.9).
source: Notably, for anterograde transport, the time spent in the fast movement state decreased substantially at sites occupied by resting mitochondria (ratio fast/slow movement states: free track - 56%/10% = 5.6 vs. occupied track - 27%/14% = 1.9).
evidence: The statement is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: For transport in the retrograde direction, the switch from fast to slow movement at occupied sites was absent (free track - 52%/8% = 6.5 vs. occupied track - 37%/4% = 9.3).
source: For transport in the retrograde direction, this switch was absent (free track - 52%/8% = 6.5 vs. occupied track - 37%/4% = 9.3).
evidence: The statement is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Retrograde transport might be less sensitive towards obstacles than anterograde transport.
source: This is in line with previous observations that retrograde transport might be less sensitive towards obstacles than anterograde transport (Mallik et al., 2004), suggesting that the slow movement state might be 'a shift to low gear' used to circumvent obstacles that the driving forces of the fast transport states have a hard time overcoming.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Mallik et al., 2004 and the data showing differential responses to obstacles.

claim: The slow movement state might be 'a shift to low gear' used to circumvent obstacles that the driving forces of the fast transport states have difficulty overcoming.
source: This is in line with previous observations that retrograde transport might be less sensitive towards obstacles than anterograde transport (Mallik et al., 2004), suggesting that the slow movement state might be 'a shift to low gear' used to circumvent obstacles that the driving forces of the fast transport states have a hard time overcoming.
evidence: The statement is presented as a speculation based on the observed data and previous literature.

claim: There are distinct foci along the axon where progress of mitochondria is slower.
source: When we plotted the time needed to advance 100 nm against the position of the repeatedly sampled axon stretch, a clear pattern emerged (Figure 3c): While progress along most of the axonal length was relatively steady (t < 1 s for traveling 100 nm), there were distinct foci where progress was slower.
evidence: The statement is supported by the repetitive tracking analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In many instances, pauses coincided with the presence of stationary mitochondria.
source: Incorporating wide-field information into the analysis, we observed that, in many instances, the pauses coincided as expected with the presence of stationary mitochondria.
evidence: The statement is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3c combining trajectory and wide-field data.

claim: Other pause foci appear on 'free' segments, suggesting additional retaining influences beyond stationary mitochondria.
source: However, other pause foci appear on 'free' segments – suggesting that there are additional retaining influences that can induce pausing, and that the clustering of pauses near stationary mitochondria might not only be merely due to geometrical constraints, but could be due to the local structure of the cytoskeleton (Bálint et al., 2013) or attractive milieu influences, such as local calcium hot spots (MacAskill and Kittler, 2010) or areas of substrate availability (Pekkurnaz et al., 2014).
evidence: The statement is supported by the data in Figure 3c and citations to potential mechanisms.

claim: The clustering of pauses near stationary mitochondria might be due to the local structure of the cytoskeleton or attractive milieu influences, such as local calcium hot spots or areas of substrate availability.
source: However, other pause foci appear on 'free' segments – suggesting that there are additional retaining influences that can induce pausing, and that the clustering of pauses near stationary mitochondria might not only be merely due to geometrical constraints, but could be due to the local structure of the cytoskeleton (Bálint et al., 2013) or attractive milieu influences, such as local calcium hot spots (MacAskill and Kittler, 2010) or areas of substrate availability (Pekkurnaz et al., 2014).
evidence: The statement is presented as speculation supported by citations to Bálint et al., 2013; MacAskill and Kittler, 2010; Pekkurnaz et al., 2014.

claim: This is the first time a feedback-based 3D SPT approach was used for tracking particles in vivo.
source: While this is the first time a feedback-based 3D SPT approach was used for tracking particles in vivo, we want to point out that this is not the only technique capable of such measurements (Shechtman et al., 2015; McHale et al., 2007), and further improvements are conceivable.
evidence: The statement is made as a claim about the novelty of the work, with acknowledgment of other potential techniques.

claim: Two-photon excitation-based tracking might in principle be more favorable for deep tissue imaging than the one-photon approach.
source: For example, two-photon excitation-based tracking might in principle be more favorable for deep tissue imaging than our one-photon approach (Helmchen and Denk, 2005).
evidence: The statement is presented as speculation supported by citation to Helmchen and Denk, 2005.

claim: The method presented is less costly than two-photon approaches and more versatile for wavelength multiplexing.
source: Still, the method presented here is less costly and – given the broad two-photon absorption cross-section of many fluorophores – more versatile as far as wavelength multiplexing is concerned.
evidence: The statement is made as a comparison based on known properties of one-photon versus two-photon excitation.

claim: Beyond the expected three major movement states of mitochondria (resting, antero- and retrograde), two components were observed: a fast and a slow transport process in both the antero- and retrograde directions.
source: Capitalizing on these technical advances, we reveal that beyond the expected three major movement states of mitochondria (resting, antero- and retrograde) previously reported in zebrafish and many other settings (Plucińska and Misgeld, 2016; Saxton and Hollenbeck, 2012), we observed two components, a fast and a slow transport process in both the antero- and retrograde directions.
evidence: The statement is supported by the data analysis in Figure 2 and citations to previous work.

claim: The fast components are consistent with the known characteristics of classical kinesin- and dynein-mediated transport reported in vivo.
source: The fast components are consistent with the known characteristics of classical kinesin- and dynein-mediated transport reported in vivo (Misgeld and Schwarz, 2017), and – even though the dynamics of organelles result from complex motor combinations and interactions – are on the order of speeds measured for these motors in reconstitution assays (0.7–1.0 μm/s; Toba et al., 2006; King and Schroer, 2000; Milo and Phillips, 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by comparison with literature values from citations.

claim: The speeds of fast components are on the order of speeds measured for kinesin and dynein motors in reconstitution assays (0.7–1.0 μm/s).
source: The fast components are consistent with the known characteristics of classical kinesin- and dynein-mediated transport reported in vivo (Misgeld and Schwarz, 2017), and – even though the dynamics of organelles result from complex motor combinations and interactions – are on the order of speeds measured for these motors in reconstitution assays (0.7–1.0 μm/s; Toba et al., 2006; King and Schroer, 2000; Milo and Phillips, 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Toba et al., 2006; King and Schroer, 2000; Milo and Phillips, 2016.

claim: The slow movement states appeared symmetrical in speed, in contrast to the fast movements.
source: The slow movement states appeared – in contrast to the fast movements – symmetrical in speed.
evidence: The statement is supported by the velocity analysis in Figure 2 and Table 1 showing similar speeds for slow anterograde and retrograde states.

claim: The transition into and out of slow movement states was not random, but followed a defined set of rules.
source: Moreover, the transition into and out of these slow movement states was not random, but followed a defined set of rules.
evidence: The statement is supported by the transition probability analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: State transitions seemed to be impacted by external influences, such as local obstacles within the axon.
source: Finally, these state transitions seemed to be impacted by external influences, such as local obstacles within the axon.
evidence: The statement is supported by the analysis in Figure 3 showing effects of stationary mitochondria on movement states.

claim: At typical sampling rates used in kymography recordings (1–2 Hz), the slow state is on the verge of detectability (duration ~0.45 s).
source: Notably, atthe typical sampling rates used in kymography recordings of mitochondrial transport in vitro or in vivo (i.e. 1–2 Hz), the slow state is on the verge of detectability (duration ~0.45 s; Table 2) – and hence might sometimes be subsumed in either the moving speeds or convolved with pause length and frequency.
evidence: The statement is supported by the measured duration of slow states in Table 1 and comparison with typical imaging rates.

claim: Shape changes of mitochondria as they encounter obstacles are unlikely to explain the slow movement state because the average displacement in the slow movement state is approximately 300 nm, which would be equivalent to a 600 nm change in overall shape.
source: However, this explanation is unlikely as the average displacement in the slow movement state is approximately 300 nm, which would be equivalent to a 600 nm change in the overall shape of the mitochondria. This is on the order of the size of moving mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: The statement is based on inference from the measured displacement data and comparison with mitochondrial size.

claim: More likely explanations of the slow movement states involve changes in the engaged molecular transport machinery.
source: Given our present data, more likely explanations of the slow movement states in our view involve changes in the engaged molecular transport machinery.
evidence: The statement is presented as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Possible explanations for slow movement states include: the engagement of additional motors beyond kinesins and dyneins, the concomitant engagement of an anchor and kinesin/dynein motors, or the existence of an unappreciated regulation that can switch the known mitochondrial motors into specific 'slow' states.
source: Options include: (I) the engagement of additional motors beyond kinesins and dyneins (the known speed characteristics of which matched the fast movement states, as expected – see Table 1), (II) the concomitant engagement of an anchor (such as syntaphilin) and kinesin/dynein motors, or (III) the existence of an unappreciated regulation that can switch the known mitochondrial motors into specific 'slow' states.
evidence: The statement presents speculative hypotheses to explain the observed slow movement states.

claim: The fact that the slow states had the same speed distribution in both directions favors the hypothesis of engagement of additional motors.
source: The fact that the slow states had the same speed distribution in both directions leads us to favor the first hypothesis; however, the nature of the involved motors remain elusive as of now.
evidence: The statement is based on inference from the symmetry of slow state velocities.

claim: One possibility for the slow movement state would be the involvement of actin-based motors in mitochondrial movements, as previously suggested based on pharmacological experiments in vitro and genetically in flies.
source: One possibility would be the involvement of actin-based motors in mitochondrial movements, as previously suggested for example based on pharmacological experiments in vitro and genetically in flies (Ligon and Steward, 2000; Morris and Hollenbeck, 1995; Pathak et al., 2010).
evidence: The statement is presented as speculation supported by citations to Ligon and Steward, 2000; Morris and Hollenbeck, 1995; Pathak et al., 2010.

claim: Myosin-actin interactions have been mostly linked to reduced mitochondrial motility.
source: Thus far, myosin-actin interactions have been mostly linked to reduced mitochondrial motility (Pathak et al., 2010) and specific stationary states, as recently demonstrated using a new opto-chemical crosslinking approach (Gutnick et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Pathak et al., 2010 and Gutnick et al., 2019.

claim: A role for a transient slow actin-dependent movement phase is compatible with the residual slow motility of mitochondria in microtubule-depleted axons in vitro and the acceleration of transport seen after myosin knock-down in flies.
source: Thus, a role for a transient slow actin-dependent movement phase that at the same time is compatible with the residual slow motility of mitochondria in microtubule-depleted axons in vitro (Morris and Hollenbeck, 1995), as well as the acceleration of transport seen after myosin knock-down in flies (Pathak et al., 2010), seems like a plausible explanation of our observations.
evidence: The statement is presented as speculation supported by citations to Morris and Hollenbeck, 1995 and Pathak et al., 2010.

claim: The slow movement state engaged preferentially when a moving mitochondrion encountered a local obstacle such as an anchored mitochondrion in the axon shaft.
source: The slow movement state engaged preferentially when a moving mitochondrion encountered a local obstacle such as an anchored mitochondrion in the axon shaft.
evidence: The statement is supported by the analysis in Figure 3 showing increased slow movement states near stationary mitochondria.

claim: Putative actin-dependent mitochondria translocations might be important for local positioning and movement between microtubule tracks.
source: This could be an indication that these putative actin-dependent mitochondria translocations are important for local positioning and movement between microtubule tracks (Gutnick et al., 2019; Atkinson et al., 1992; Langford, 1995) and the notion that myosin-actin interactions increase mitochondrial pause frequencies (Morris and Hollenbeck, 1995; Pathak et al., 2010).
evidence: The statement is presented as speculation supported by citations to Gutnick et al., 2019; Atkinson et al., 1992; Langford, 1995; Morris and Hollenbeck, 1995; Pathak et al., 2010.

claim: The convenience of gene overexpression and deletion in zebrafish combined with 3D orbital tracking allows testing of hypotheses about molecular mechanisms of slow movement states.
source: While this specific molecular interpretation remains speculative, the convenience of gene overexpression and deletion in zebrafish combined with 3D orbital tracking now allows testing of this hypothesis.
evidence: The statement is based on known capabilities of zebrafish as a model system and the demonstrated tracking approach.

claim: The observation of new movement states for mitochondria testifies to the power of the in vivo 3D SPT approach.
source: In any case, while the exact molecular nature and role of the slow movement phases of mitochondrial trafficking remain to be resolved, the observation of new movement states for a well-studied organelle such as mitochondria testifies to the power of the in vivo 3D SPT approach.
evidence: The statement is an inference based on the discovery of previously undetected movement states.

claim: Applications include investigations using neurological disease models, such as tauopathies, where transitions of movement states and the duty cycle between movement and stationary phases seem to be especially affected.
source: Indeed, we foresee a range of applications, including investigations using neurological disease models, such as tauopathies, where transitions of movement states and hence the duty cycle between movement and stationary phases seem to be especially affected (Plucińska et al., 2012; Fatouros et al., 2012; Devireddy et al., 2015).
evidence: The statement is presented as a potential application supported by citations to Plucińska et al., 2012; Fatouros et al., 2012; Devireddy et al., 2015.

claim: The ability to visualize the cellular surroundings of a trafficking organelle will allow detailed determination of how neuronal landmarks modulate mitochondrial behavior.
source: For instance, the ability to visualize the cellular surroundings of a trafficking organelle will allow a detailed determination of how neuronal landmarks known to be preferentially associated with mitochondria, such as branch points (Faits et al., 2016; Courchet et al., 2013; Spillane et al., 2013) or presynaptic terminals (Lewis et al., 2016; Obashi and Okabe, 2013), modulate mitochondrial behavior.
evidence: The statement is presented as a potential application supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The approach can be readily combined with organelle-targeted biosensors and optogenetic actuators of organelle physiology.
source: This approach can be readily combined with a rapidly expanding set of organelle-targeted biosensors (Breckwoldt et al., 2014) and optogenetic actuators of organelle physiology (Rost et al., 2015; Ashrafi et al., 2014), as well as motor (Gutnick et al., 2019; van Bergeijk et al., 2015) and track (Borowiak et al., 2015) composition.
evidence: The statement is presented as a potential application supported by citations to relevant tools.

claim: The laser beam orbited about a single organelle provides optical selectivity and will enable detailed correlation between the physiological state of a trafficking organelle and its movement behavior.
source: As the laser beam is orbited about a single organelle, it provides optical selectively and will enable a detailed correlation between the physiological state of a trafficking organelle and its movement behavior.
evidence: The statement is based on the technical capabilities of the orbital tracking approach.

claim: The system achieved precise hardware synchronization using a field programmable gate array and sub millisecond timing of the tracking feedback loop algorithm by executing on a real-time operating system.
source: We obtained precise hardware synchronization using a field programable gate array as well as sub millisecond timing of the tracking feedback loop algorithm by executing the algorithm on a real-time operating system.
evidence: The statement describes technical implementation details of the microscope system.

claim: The lateral tracking range was increased to centimeters by amending the 3D orbital tracking algorithm with a long-range tracking feature that automatically re-centers the sample stage.
source: We increased the lateral tracking range to centimeters by amending the 3D orbital tracking algorithm with a long-range tracking feature that automatically re-centers the sample stage before the particle exits the field-of-view.
evidence: The statement describes a technical improvement to the microscope system.

claim: Multiple laser lines were incorporated into the orbit light path, including a 405 nm laser for controlled photo-activation.
source: We incorporated multiple laser lines into the orbit light path – including a 405 nm laser for controlled photo-activation, which allows single organelle tracking in a densely labeled background.
evidence: The statement describes a technical feature of the microscope system.

claim: Dark orbits were implemented to decrease photobleaching and phototoxicity, which significantly extends experiment duration in exchange for a moderate decrease in temporal resolution.
source: To decrease photobleaching and phototoxicity, we implemented dark orbits, where only a subset of orbits is illuminated by the excitation laser, which significantly extends experiment duration in exchange for a moderate decrease in temporal resolution.
evidence: The statement describes a technical feature and its trade-offs.

claim: The combination of technical advances makes it possible to track single organelles in a living organism in 3D with nanometer scale spatial resolution, millisecond scale temporal resolution and over lateral distances of centimeters.
source: This combination of technical advances makes it possible to track single organelles in a living organism in 3D with nanometer scale spatial resolution, millisecond scale temporal resolution and over lateral distances of centimeters.
evidence: The statement summarizes the capabilities demonstrated by the experimental results.

claim: Stem axons nearby blood vessels exhibited low-amplitude fluctuations perpendicular to mitochondrial movement due to the heartbeat.
source: For example, stem axons nearby blood vessels exhibited low-amplitude fluctuations perpendicular to mitochondrial movement due to the heartbeat (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: The shape of the mitochondria did not impact tracking precision.
source: We also verified that the shape of the mitochondria did not impact our tracking precision (Material and methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The statement is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Moving mitochondria in zebrafish show an average length of 0.71 ± 0.13 µm.
source: As moving mitochondria in zebrafish show an average length of 0.71 ± 0.13 µm, we can rule out an influence of the mitochondrial shape on localization precision.

claim: The obtained velocity values from 3D Orbital tracking are consistent with a previous study when accounting for differences in time resolution and temperature.
source: To validate the measured values, we compared the average velocities of motion in the anterograde and retrograde direction with results of a previous study (Plucińska et al., 2012). The obtained values of the 3D Orbital tracking approach are consistent with the previous study when accounting for the difference in time resolution (10 ms versus 500 ms, leading to the inability to properly discriminate between fast and slow components in the previous study) and temperature (25°C here versus 28°C in Plucińska et al., 2012, Table 2).
evidence: The statement is supported by comparison with published data from Plucińska et al., 2012 shown in Table 2.

source: To estimate the photoactivation contrast, we converted five sensory neurons and measured the PAGFP and TagRFP-T channels before and after photoactivation. This resulted in a ~ 25 fold change in ratio (27.8 ± 2.3; red channel, before-to-after: 0.7 ± 0.05; green channel: 20.6 ± 1.5; mean ±sem = 5 cells).
evidence: The statement is supported by measurements from the experimental protocol.
